title: Medical Necessity, Documentation, and Querying

sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain medical necessity and how payers apply it to coverage and payment.
- Relate documentation to code assignment, including specificity, sequencing, and supporting source documents.
- Describe compliant querying of clinicians through proper channels when documentation is unclear, conflicting, or incomplete.
- Recognize the assistant's support role and scope-of-practice boundaries in documentation and querying.
- Apply the principle of never assuming, and escalate or query rather than guessing or altering records.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of medical necessity like needing a real reason before the school lets you leave early: the service has to be something that truly helps diagnose or treat a health problem, not just something someone wants.

### Question 2

The insurance company is like a referee that checks whether the care was truly needed using its rulebook; it does not just take anyone's word for it.

### Question 3

A service is like a ticket that only works if the reason for it is real; if the reason is missing, the ticket does not get paid.

### Question 4

Writing down the real reason for a visit is like writing the reason on a permission slip; it explains why the care happened and proves it was needed.

### Question 5

Being on the menu does not mean the meal is right for every person; a covered service still has to fit this patient's actual health need.

### Question 6

Medical necessity is like needing a genuine health reason: fixing a real problem counts, but changing how something looks just for fun does not.

### Question 7

“Reasonable and necessary” is like asking, “Is this a sensible thing to do for this health problem?” before agreeing to pay.

### Question 8

The visit note is like the story of what happened and why; without that story, nobody can tell if the visit was truly needed.

### Question 9

The diagnosis is like the label on a box that explains why you opened it; it shows the payer the medical reason behind the care.

### Question 10

A necessity denial is like a referee saying, “I don't see enough proof this was needed”; it is about the evidence, not the equipment.

### Question 11

Coverage is like a library having a certain book on its shelf; necessity is whether that book is actually the right one for this reader's need.

### Question 12

The doctor or clinician is like the person who decides a repair is needed after inspecting the problem; the assistant helps write up and submit the paperwork.

### Question 13

If a homework paper is missing the answer, you ask the teacher, not copy a classmate's answer; the assistant asks the clinician rather than guessing.

### Question 14

An ABN is like a heads-up note saying, “This might not be paid for; you may have to cover it yourself” before the service happens.

### Question 15

Bigger, costlier services are like bigger purchases that need more proof they are truly needed before they get approved.

### Question 16

The chief complaint is like the first line of a story that explains why the visit happened at all.

### Question 17

Needing a medicine is not like borrowing a friend's favorite snack; the clinician has to confirm it is right for this patient.

### Question 18

Experimental treatments are like a recipe that has not been tested yet; insurers usually wait until it is proven safe and useful before paying.

### Question 19

LCDs and NCDs are like the official rulebook that explains exactly when Medicare will agree a service is needed.

### Question 20

A test with no question written down still needs the question; the payer needs the documented reason for the exam, not just that it happened.

### Question 21

Screening is like a routine smoke-alarm check when nothing seems wrong; diagnostic is like investigating after the alarm actually goes off.

### Question 22

The record is like the proof of work for a school project; if it is messy, missing pieces, or turned in late, it cannot prove what was really done.

### Question 23

A clinical indication is like the doctor writing “because the patient has a sore throat and fever” next to a throat-swab order.

### Question 24

An order is like a wish list; the insurance still checks each item against its rules before agreeing to pay.

### Question 25

The assistant is like a careful helper who makes sure all the paperwork is right and raises a hand when something looks off, without making the doctor's decisions.

### Question 26

A procedure with no reason in the chart is like an answer with no question; it leaves the payer with nothing to justify the charge.

### Question 27

Managing a chronic condition is like keeping a garden tended over time; regular check-ins are genuinely needed, not optional.

### Question 28

A reviewer checks the “why” behind the care, like a teacher checking the reasoning behind an answer rather than how neatly the page looks.

### Question 29

Coding from an assumption is like filling in a blank answer you were never given; it might look complete but it is not true.

### Question 30

CDI is like proofreading an important story so every true detail is included clearly, making sure nothing important is missing or wrong.

### Question 31

Coding is like answering a test using only the textbook page in front of you, not from memory or wishful thinking.

### Question 32

If a chore is not written on the list, you cannot prove you did it; the medical record is that list.

### Question 33

The visit note is like the page of a diary for that day; you code from today's page, not from someone else's.

### Question 34

To know what was built, you read the builder's notes, not a rumor about another project.

### Question 35

A superbill is like a shopping list jotted quickly; you still check it against the actual receipt (the record) before paying.

### Question 36

Saying “left knee” instead of just “knee” is like naming the exact drawer where something is; ICD-10 codes often need that detail.

### Question 37

Before a doctor is sure, the outpatient chart records the clues (like “fever”) rather than guessing the final answer.

### Question 38

Sequencing is like putting the main character first in a story lineup, then the supporting characters in the right order.

### Question 39

It is like choosing the most precise label that the evidence actually proves, not the fanciest label you can imagine.

### Question 40

If you don't yet know the final answer, you write down the clues you do have (the symptoms) instead of making up an answer.

### Question 41

A long-running condition that still affects care is like an ongoing class on your schedule; it stays on the list while it matters.

### Question 42

A history code is like a “previously owned” note that still matters for how the car (or patient) is cared for now.

### Question 43

An E/M note is like a receipt itemizing the thinking and work that went into the visit, which decides the level billed.

### Question 44

A more complicated visit is like a harder puzzle; the note must show the harder thinking to justify the higher level.

### Question 45

Time-based coding is like billing by the hour; you must actually write down the time spent on real work, not guess it.

### Question 46

A procedure note is like a recipe's step-by-step record; without the actual steps and the part involved, the code cannot be verified.

### Question 47

A modifier is like a note in the margin of a form that explains a special circumstance, but only if it is true.

### Question 48

An unspecified code is like writing “somewhere on the arm” when you do not know exactly where; it is only used when you truly lack the detail.

### Question 49

The problem list is like a to-do list; an item still has to be worked on during today's visit to count for today.

### Question 50

When two notes disagree, you ask the person who wrote them to explain, rather than picking whichever one you like.

### Question 51

MDM is like measuring how hard the doctor had to think, based on how many problems, how much data, and how much risk was involved.

### Question 52

Adding a diagnosis that is not in the chart is like writing an answer the teacher never gave; it looks complete but it is not honest.

### Question 53

The note comes first, like measuring a room before writing down its size; the code simply reports what was already documented.

### Question 54

These components are like the chapters of the visit story, and together they show how much work the visit required.

### Question 55

A lab report is like the photo proof that backs up what the doctor suspected, making the diagnosis solid.

### Question 56

Authentication is like signing your name on your homework so everyone knows it is yours and you stand behind it.

### Question 57

An external cause code is like writing “from falling off a bike” next to “broken arm” to explain how it happened.

### Question 58

When the instructions are unclear, you ask the person who wrote them rather than guessing, so the final answer is correct.

### Question 59

If a form needs the exact street but you only know the city, you ask for the street; if you cannot get it, you write only what you know.

### Question 60

A query is like raising your hand to ask the teacher to explain an unclear instruction, so your answer is based on the right information.

### Question 61

You ask for clarification when a form is missing or confusing, not because you simply want a different answer.

### Question 62

Proper channels are like using the school's official form instead of shouting across the room; it makes sure the question reaches the right person correctly.

### Question 63

A good question is like asking “What happened here?” while showing the clues, instead of whispering the answer you want.

### Question 64

Including the clues is like showing the doctor the specific page with the confusing part, so they can answer precisely.

### Question 65

Only the person who wrote the note can explain what they meant, just like only the author can explain their own book.

### Question 66

If a note says “arm” but not which arm, you ask which arm rather than guessing or charging for both.

### Question 67

A linkage query is like asking whether a leak caused the water damage or the two are unrelated, because the answer changes the code.

### Question 68

A query should stick to the clues already in the story, not whisper new clues that were never there.

### Question 69

Asking during the project is “concurrent”; asking after it is done is “retrospective”—both seek the missing detail.

### Question 70

A leading query is like prompting, “The answer is X, right?” instead of asking, “What did you actually find?”

### Question 71

If a line is blank, you ask the author to fill it in, rather than copying from a different form.

### Question 72

A verbal clarification is like a phone call about a homework question; you still write down the answer so it is not lost.

### Question 73

POA is like marking whether a stain was on the shirt before it was washed or appeared during the wash.

### Question 74

Confirming the reason is like making sure the “because” is written next to every action, so the code makes sense.

### Question 75

If a teacher does not answer your question, you follow the classroom rule to ask again or tell the principal, not answer it yourself.

### Question 76

The assistant is like the messenger who notices a missing detail and delivers the question, without writing the answer.

### Question 77

A good query is like offering a menu based on the clues rather than pushing one specific dish.

### Question 78

Guessing when unsure is like writing an answer you made up; asking is always safer than assuming.

### Question 79

Fixing a typo before turning in the paper is better than after it is graded; querying early saves trouble.

### Question 80

If asked to write an answer that is not supported, the honest move is to say no and ask for the real information through the correct route.

### Question 81

The clarified answer is added correctly to the story, like fixing a line without tearing out the original page.

### Question 82

A query is asking “what really happened?” while improper alteration is telling someone “make it say this.”

### Question 83

If two papers disagree about which side, you ask which one is correct rather than splitting the difference.

### Question 84

Keeping the question and answer is like keeping your scratch work; it proves how you reached the final answer.

### Question 85

The good question asks which type it is; the bad ones hint at the answer they want.

### Question 86

CDI is like making sure the whole true story is written down clearly, with queries used to fill in honest missing details.

### Question 87

A query is built only from the clues already in the chart, like a detective who works from evidence, not hunches.

### Question 88

If the description is too fuzzy to file, you ask the author for the precise wording instead of filing it under “miscellaneous.”

### Question 89

The whole system works like an honest report card: the work is documented, checked for necessity, and clarified when unclear, so the final grade is accurate.
